title.narrative: Human Rights, Inclusion and Empowerment Trust Fund 2020-2026
Human Rights, Inclusion and Empowerment Trust Fund 2020-2026

description.narrative:
Sida GLOBAL/DEMO has an ongoing agreement (SEK 20 million per year) with the Human Rights, Inclusion and Empowerment Umbrella Trust Fund (HRIETF), which will soon formally be renamed the Human Rights Trust Fund (HRTF). The financial component of the agreement between the fund and Sida will expire at the end of June 2026 (the World Bank operates on a fiscal year from 1 July to 30 June). The agreement was extended by two years in 2024, covering 2024 and 2025, with an additional allocation of SEK 40 million in total, distributed as SEK 20 million per year. Sida is the largest donor to the fund other donors include Canada, Finland, Iceland, the Netherlands, Norway, the United Kingdom, and France.
The HRTF is a multi-donor trust fund dedicated to enhancing the understanding and application of human rights principles in the World Bank Groups (WBG) work. Established in 2008, the HRTF has evolved into a trusted institutional resource within the WBG, providing expert advisory support to task teams across all regions and sectors. The HRTF aims to strengthen human rights in development by directly funding human rights initiatives through Bank executed grants. The grant work, and its lessons, embed human rights principles in ongoing World Bank projects and generate practical knowledge that strengthens the integration of human rights. By leveraging strategic insights, conducting comprehensive grant related work, and sharing best practices, the HRTF offers a dedicated platform for embedding human rights principles into development analysis and operations. HRTF organizes its work around the two core pillars of its mandate: Pillar 1: Enhance the understanding of human rights in development and Pillar 2: Enhance the application of human rights.
As part of pillar 1, the trust fund focuses on two main streams of work: it organizes workshops, events and trainings on human rights in development for World Bank staff, and it fosters exchange and collaboration with internal and external partners to advance the understanding of human rights in the context of all sectors of development.
The second pillar of the trust funds work consists of the allocation of grants to project teams. The grants program of the HRTF has four thematic funding windows that reflect the strategic priorities of the trust fund: 1. Infrastructure 2. Governance, inclusive institutions, and empowerment 3. Fragility, conflict, violence, and forced displacement and 4. Social inclusion.

Fonden för mänskliga rättigheter, inkludering och Empowerment (Human Rights, Inclusion and Empowerment Fund) – HRIETF är en fond inom Världsbanken (VB) vars verksamhet bygger på erfarenheter och lärdomar (utvärdering gjord 2017) från den tidigare Nordic Trust Fund (NTF).
HRIETF har ett WBG (World Bank Group)-mandat och dess övergripande mål är att "öka och stärka förståelsen och tillämpningen av principerna för mänskliga rättigheter i WBG´s arbete". Genom tekniskt och finansiellt stöd vill HRIETF öka den interna kunskapen om mänskliga rättigheter och hur mänskliga rättigheter kan integreras i Världsbankens verksamhet. För att uppnå detta avser HRIETF att arbeta strategiskt med WBG ledarskap/chefskap för att säkerställa att mänskliga rättigheter inkluderas och integreras på institutionell nivå i organisationen. Dess syfte är även att ge finansiellt bidrag till VBs landskontor och tematiska enheter på huvudkontoret för att integrera mänskliga rättigheter i sin verksamhet. Fonden kommer också att fokusera sitt arbete på kommunikation, kunskapshantering, lärande och partnerskapsbyggande. HRIETF kommer arbeta genom sex tematiska fönster för att nå sitt övergripande mål; 1)Demokrati, Institutioner och Empowerment, 2) Infrastruktur, 3) ) Sårbarhet, Konflikt, Våld och Tvångsförflyttning, 4) Forskning och Utvärdering) och 5) Social Inkludering samt 6) Programhantering och Administration.
HRIETF är ett ”kunskaps- och lärande” initiativ som inrättades 2009 av Danmark, Finland, Island, Norge och Sverige och senare anslöt sig även Tyskland. Fonden har haft sin organisatoriska hemvist på olika enheter inom VB genom åren. I oktober 2019 påbörjade ett organisatoriskt förändringsarbete inom banken vilket i förlängningen kom att innebära att fonden flyttats från Governance avdelningen till avdelningen för Social Utveckling.
NTF´s övergripande mål var att hjälpa banken att ”utveckla en ökad uppfattning om hur de mänskliga rättigheterna förhåller sig till organisationens analytiska och operativa verksamhet”. Dess verksamhet var att utforska och identifiera innovativa metoder för att integrera rättighetsperspektivet i organisationen för att nå VB-målet att minska fattigdomen och öka det gemensamma välståndet. NTF gav ekonomiskt bidrag till VBs landkontor samt enheter på huvudkontoret och bidrog med tekniskt stöd till Världsbanks team för att utforska sambandet mellan deras arbete och mänskliga rättigheter. Sedan 2010 har fonden godkänt 111 bidrag i fem bidrags-rundor, genomsnitt US $240 000 och med ett maximalt beviljande av US $450 000.
I denna nya fas har HRIETF, vidareutvecklat tre strategier som fokuserar på kommunikation, kunskapshantering, lärande och partnerskap. Kommunikationsstrategin är inriktad mot identifiering av viktiga målgrupper och partners med syfte att på ett strategiskt vis kommunicera verksamheten samt dess resultat. Den övergripande målsättningen för kunskapshantering och lärande är att öka tillämpningen av mänskliga rättigheter i och utanför projektbidragen och därigenom bidra till att lärandet institutionaliseras. Den tredje strategin är partnerskapsstrategin som omfattar partnerskap mellan både externa och interna partners.
The Nordic Trust Fund (NTF), har nu bytt namn till HRIETF utvärderades 2017 (2009 - 2017). Sammanfattningsvis har NTF bidragit till att minska vissa av spänningarna som relaterar till mänskliga rättigheter inom VB. VB-team har integrerat mänskliga rättighet i sitt arbete på ett sätt som har upplevts som stärkande. De ekonomiska bidragen (grants) har bidragit till att bygga kunskap bland VB-team när det gäller att genomföra projekt och påverka attityder och beteenden i relation till mänskliga rättigheter. Projekt har lett till institutionell förändring inom VB, till exempel antagandet av strategin för sexuell orientering och könsidentitet samt både antagande och implementering av ramverket för miljö och socialfrågor som uttryckligen hänvisar till mänskliga rättigheter.
Sidas erfarenhet av att samarbeta med fonden har varit positiv. Dialogen med sekretariatet och andra givare har varit produktiv och robust. Resultaten av kontinuerlig och tät diskussion speglas i det nya och förstärkta projektdokument där resultatstyrning förstärkts och strategin för projekt (grants) har omarbetats och är nu mer systematisk och strategisk. Det kvarstår utmaningar som reflekteras i de identifierade dialogfrågorna samt i riskerna. Dialogfrågor kommer Sida att driva i dialog med banken, fondens sekretariat och andra givare under avtalsperioden.
VB har genom olika initativ svarat mot covid -19 pandemin. Fonden för diskussioner internt om hur man på bästa sätt ska involvera fondens aktiviteter i responsen. I det nästkommande PC (sept. 2020) kommer frågan att diskutteras i mer detalj.

The World Bank Group (WBG) through the Human Rights, Inclusion and Empowerment Trust Fund (HRIETF ) is mandated and committed (through its five institutions) to reduce poverty and increase shared prosperity (Twin-goals). The HRIETF follows on from the Nordic Trust Fund (NTF) and is based on discussions with the NTF donors during the second quarter 2019. The HRIETF is placed within the WBG at the Social Development Practice. The HRIETF has a WBG mandate, and the development objective of the TF is: “increase and strengthen the understanding and application of human rights principles in the WBG´s work”. Through technical and financial support, the HRIETF want to scale up internal capacity on human rights. It aims to work strategically with the WBG management to ensure institutional advancement of human rights in its operations. In addition, the HRIETF will provide grants to WB teams (WBG Country Management Units at country level and to WBG practices at the headquarters) to integrate human rights into its operations. It will also scale- its communication and knowledge management & learning work. The HRIETF has sexthematic windows in which it aims to operate; 1) Governance, Inclusive Institutions and Empowerment, 2) Infrastructure, 3) Fragility, Conflict, Violence and Forced Displacement, 4) Research and Evaluation, 5) Social Inclusion and 6) Program management and Administration.The HRIETF is a knowledge and learning initiative established in 2009 by Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden, and joined later by Germany. The mandate of the NTF was to help the Bank develop an informed view of how human rights relate to its analytical and operational activities. Its objectives were to explore and identify innovative approaches for incorporating human rights perspectives and empowering vulnerable groups to help make WBG analysis and operations more effective in reducing poverty and boosting shared prosperity. It did so through a grant program that provided financial and technical support to World Bank teams interested in exploring the link between their work and human rights. Since 2010 the grant program has approved 111 grants in five grant rounds, averaging US$ 240,000 and with a maximum grant of US$ 450,000.In addition to the programme document, the Secretariat has developed three strategies that focuses on Communication, Knowledge Management and Learning and Partnerships. The communication strategy is centered on identification of key audiences and partners for communicating results. The Knowledge Management and Learning strategy overall goal is to increase the uptake of human rights in and beyond the grants, thereby contributing to learning being captured and institutionalized. The third strategy is the partnership strategy which encompasses Trust Fund wider partnerships.In 2017 the Nordic Trust Fund (NTF), now HRIETF (name change in 2020) was evaluated (2009 - 2017). In sum, the NTF has contributed to alleviating some of the tensions with respect to human rights issues within the WBG. Sida´s experience engaging with the TF has been positive. The dialogue with the secretariat and other donors have been productive and robust. The results of these discussion can be mirrored in the new and strengthened project document where results based managed has been reinforced and the strategy for grant making has been modified and is now more systematic and strategic. Several challenges however remain; the TF ability to demonstrate results on impact level is one such example. The identified dialogue issues will be important to explicitly emphasize in the upcoming agreement period.Covid -19 has had severe impact on our whole society. The World Bank Group has put in place a response. The role of the TF in this response is not clear. It is however something Sida aims to follow closely in dialogue with the Secretariat but also to raise in the upcoming PC.

title.narrative: Beslut om insats, VB Human Rights, Inclusion and Empowerment Trust Fund 2020-2022

description.narrative:
During FY2025, the HRTF supported 25 task teams that conducted activities across 13 countries and across all regions. The grant teams established partnerships with 127 diverse actors, including local governments, civil society organizations, regional stakeholders, and community based organizations. Fourteen of the 25 grants were connected to World Bank financing projects with a total financing envelope of US $1 billion. By providing technical assistance, evidence based analysis, capacity building on human rights, among others, grant teams contributed to policy change in at least 28 national or subnational laws and policies. Grant teams strengthened legal and institutional frameworks by developing legal tools and manuals, building institutional capacity, and embedding rights based approaches into governance processes, ensuring effective implementation of laws and alignment with international human rights standards. Their work promoted equality and inclusion for marginalized groups including women, persons with disabilities, migrants, refugees, and SOGIESC communities while improving human rights based data systems through new tools, dashboards, and participatory feedback platforms. They also advanced the knowledge base, producing at least 30 analytical products. Collectively, these efforts are assessed to have deepened inclusive development and reinforced human rights based approaches across operations in different contexts.
Throughout FY2025, the HRTF expanded awareness and operational understanding of human rights across the WBG by leveraging global observances, engaging leadership, and creating learning opportunities. , cohosted high level events on AI and disability rights, and launched the self paced Human Rights in Development online course alongside other training sessions and podcasts that reached staff worldwide. The Secretariat also launched the inaugural Human Rights Champions Award Grant. Grant teams delivered 69 knowledge events to empower marginalized groups, influenced national policy reforms, and promote inclusive, participatory decision making.
The following grant examples illustrate the HRTFs on the ground impact: Advancing Disability Rights: Over a Decade of HRTF Grants. HRTF grants have helped transform how development programs address the rights of persons with disabilities, with efforts grounded in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) and contributing to broader institutional shifts such as the World Banks Disability Inclusion and Accountability Framework. In Egypt, an HRTF funded activities overhauled the disability assessment system from a medical to a human rights based model, ensuring fairer access to social protection benefits. In Bhutan, a HRTF grant enabled cities to retrofit public buses and stops with ramps, improving mobility for people with disabilities, while in East Africa, grants strengthened inclusive education through safer routes to school, classroom materials, and CRPD aligned teacher training. Building on this momentum, the 2025 Global Disability Summit saw the launch of the Disability Data Hub co-funded by the HRTF which provides tools and indicators across seven sectors in 63 countries. By highlighting gaps and opportunities in areas such as employment, education, and health, the Hub is driving more informed, accountable, and human rights based development.
Environmental Access Rights. An HRTF grant provided technical support to governments in their efforts at implementing the Escazú Agreement, Latin America and the Caribbeans landmark treaty on access rights, information, participation, and justice in environmental matters. The activities funded by the grant have been pivotal in turning highlevel commitments into concrete actions. In Argentina, the grant funded a comprehensive baseline assessment of gaps in transparency and protection for environmental defenders, which became the basis of Argentinas first national Escazú implementation roadmap. Belize is similarly using HRTF funded analysis to finalize its national strategy, and in Brazil the research has mapped out steps toward compliance once Brazil ratifies the treaty. The grant also jumpstarted work in Colombia by supporting a diagnosis of participation rights, which will inform Colombias Escazú implementation roadmap. HRTF sponsorship of environment defender forums enabled grassroots advocates to shape the first ever Regional Action Plan to protect environmental defenders, which was adopted by Escazú member states at COP3 in April 2024.
Inclusion of Venezuelan Migrants. With support from the HRTF, Ecuador, Colombia, and Peru advanced migrant inclusion by recognizing Venezuelans as rightsholders and active contributors. In Ecuador, reforms eased degree recognition especially for women boosting access to skilled jobs, while national campaigns and economic evidence shifted public attitudes and policy toward inclusion. In Colombia, local governments embedded long term integration into development plans, improved data systems, and enabled over 2 million Venezuelans to access social services and formal employment through implementation of a regularization scheme. In Perú, the focus turned to building up the institutions and public services that would realize human and migrants rights, through launching a national strategy for integrating migrants and refugees, providing guidance to schools, and training media to tell migration stories with nuance and care. The HRTF grants on Venezuelan migrants have catalyzed over 4 billion dollars in additional public investment across LAC.
Inclusive Participation in Pakistans Newly Merged Districts. In Pakistans Newly Merged Districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, an area shaped by fragility, restrictive gender norms, and limited civic space, an HRTF grant is helping realize the right to participate in public affairs through inclusive local governance reform. Grounded in CEDAW, ICCPR General Comment No. 25, OHCHR guidelines on participation, and Pakistans Universal Periodic Review commitments, the grant applies human rights based analytics to improve participatory planning gender responsive budgeting, and accountability. A major achievement has been the development of training manuals for womens subcommittees in village councils, which strengthened womens direct engagement in governance and informed a new provincial requirement mandating women as cosignatories on Village Council bank accounts a milestone reform that institutionalizes womens role in financial oversight. The project also introduced a management information system and community feedback mechanisms that enhance transparency and ensure local voices inform governance, service delivery, and the World Bank financed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Rural Investment and Institutional Support Project.
A participatory climate risk assessment manual developed under an HRTF grant grounded in a human rights based and participatory approach has guided implementation of the USD 132 million ProClimat project in the Republic of Congo. The manuals climate risk analyses have been incorporated into local implementation plans worth USD 17 million. It has also informed the USD 90 million EKPENGBA project in the Central African Republic, supporting climate resilient smallscale infrastructure and advocacy efforts that are now influencing national guidelines for local development planning.
In Nigeria, it assisted the national disability commission in aligning its strategies with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), strengthening the implementation of inclusive policies at the national level.
In Somalia, limited data on healthcare access and weak integration of human rights principles have contributed to disparities affecting women, children, marginalized groups, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and nomadic communities. An HRTF grant supported the integration of human rights into the national Female Health Worker Program under the World Banks Recurrent Cost and Reform Financing III Project. The initiative adapted service delivery to better meet the needs of marginalized populations. ICT based feedback tools strengthened community engagement, while disaggregated data helped identify gaps and guide mobile health outreach. A real time data dashboard now supports district level planning. More than 1,400 female health workers and supervisors, along with over 18 government officials, were trained in human rights principles, including the rights to health, equality, and accountability. Training materials were institutionalized in national health programming and referenced in updated program guidance.The project also strengthened institutional capacity through collaboration with the Ministry of Health, UNFPA, and UNICEF, and supported revisions to key national policy documents. Early results indicate expanded service coverage and stronger community participation particularly among women, children, IDPs, and nomadic populations demonstrating that inclusive, datadriven approaches can advance health rights in fragile contexts.
The Indigenous Peoples Resilience Framework identifies key factors that enable Indigenous Peoples to withstand climate change and other external shocks. It is based on qualitative research conducted by Indigenous researchers across 16 countries. Supported by the HRTF, the framework is already influencing how climate adaptation is understood and implemented, both within the World Bank and in international policy forums.
